title: Fire in your building
lede: The alarm is going, or you smell smoke, or someone is banging on doors. There is a strong pull to work out whether this is real before doing anything.

blocks.text: The alarm is going, or you smell smoke, or someone is banging on doors. There is a strong pull to work out whether this is real before doing anything.

items: Smoke kills far more people than flame, and it is fast — a corridor can go from hazy to unsurvivable in a couple of minutes. Time spent verifying is taken directly from your escape window.
The dangerous instinct is normalcy bias: gathering belongings, getting dressed, finishing the call. It is well documented in fire deaths and it feels entirely reasonable at the time.
Every second of hesitation costs more than any object you own.

items.move: Get out now; do not investigate
items.detail: Take keys and a phone if they are within reach. Nothing else. Not the laptop, not the documents.

items.move: Test doors with the back of your hand before opening
items.detail: Hot door means fire on the other side. Do not open it. Find another route.
The survivable air is near the floor. Crawl if you must, and keep one hand on a wall so you can navigate in zero visibility.
They fail, they open onto the fire floor, and they fill with smoke.
Every closed door buys minutes for whoever is still inside.

items.move: If you cannot get out, make a safe room and signal
items.detail: Seal the gaps with wet fabric, go to a window, call and give your exact floor and room. Being locatable is what gets you rescued.

items.say: "Fire at 14 Oakfield Road. I am on the fourth floor, front of the building, one adult and a child. We cannot reach the stairs."
"Fire — get out now." Two words while you move. Do not stop to explain.
A direct instruction with their name and a physical action: "Sam. Take my hand. Walk."

items: Going back in for anything at all, including pets, once you are out. This is a leading cause of death in building fires.
Opening a hot door to see how bad it is.
Assuming it is a drill because it usually is.
Getting dressed properly or gathering documents.
Go to the assembly point and be counted. Rescuers make life-risking decisions based on who is unaccounted for.
Get checked for smoke inhalation even if you feel fine. Damage presents hours later.
Photograph everything for insurance once permitted back, and get the incident report number.
Locate your two nearest exits wherever you sleep tonight and every night after. This is the lesson that actually saves you next time.
